resources.string: More Settings
Connection
Choose how and when to connect. Keep the defaults if your connection works.
Advanced Protocols
Special connection options. Most people can leave these unchanged. Unavailable options depend on the selected protocol.
Privacy & Security
Protect connection details and control what happens when the tunnel stops.
Network & Routing
Choose which apps and destinations use the tunnel and how names are resolved.
Proxy & Chaining
Use local proxies, connect through another proxy, or share the tunnel on your network.
Organization / Zero Trust
Connect with an organization account. Personal connections can leave these settings empty.
Performance
Adjust recovery, speed and connection checks. Change these only to solve a problem.
Help
Explanations for the controls in Configurations and More Settings.

Choose a tunnel type. Smart Connect tests the available protocols and selects a working route.
Turbo finds a route quickly. More thorough scans may improve endpoint selection but take longer to connect.
Connect apps that support a proxy. This mode does not route the whole device through a VPN.
HTTP/2 works over TCP and suits many restricted networks. Try HTTP/3 when UDP is available.
Changes WireGuard traffic patterns to help on restricted networks. Stronger settings can reduce speed.
Leave empty to find a gateway automatically. A fixed IP:port can help on a known network but may stop working later.
Use a fixed HTTP/2 gateway when automatic discovery fails. Leave empty for automatic selection.
First gateway of a two-hop connection. Leave empty for automatic selection; both hops must use different IP addresses.
Second gateway and exit of a two-hop connection. A bad override can prevent the tunnel from connecting.
Sends a small packet to keep idle connections open. Shorter intervals use more battery and data; 1–120 seconds, default 5.
Paste a trusted ECH configuration in base64 form. An incorrect value can prevent MASQUE handshakes.
Smaller pieces may pass a restricted handshake but add overhead. Use 1–16384 bytes or a range such as 100-200.
Wait between handshake pieces. Higher values slow connection setup; 0–100 ms or a range such as 1-5.
Time allowed to detect a destination name for routing. Longer waits may delay new connections; 1–5000 ms.
Fixed loopback endpoints in Proxy mode, available only on this device. Both use the same tunnel. Set either address in a compatible app.
Saved SOCKS5 listener for Device VPN mode. Proxy mode uses the fixed address above without changing this saved value.
Organization name supplied by your administrator. Changing it selects a separate organization identity.
Enrollment token supplied by your administrator. Use this or the two service token fields below.
Identifier of a service token. Both its ID and secret are required.
Secret paired with the service token ID. It stays on this device and is excluded from settings backups.
Email sign-in is unavailable in this app. Use an enrollment token or a service token instead.
IPv4 is the most compatible choice. Select IPv6 only if the current network supports it.
Time to test a candidate gateway. Lower values may reject slow working routes; 1–60 seconds, empty uses the default.
Time allowed for a MASQUE handshake. Raise it on slow networks; 1–60 seconds, empty uses the default.
Wait before the tunnel tries to recover. Shorter waits retry sooner; 1–30 seconds, empty uses the default.

Device VPN protects every app on this phone by routing all traffic through Aethon — nothing to set up in other apps. Proxy mode instead keeps normal traffic as-is and offers two local addresses (HTTP and SOCKS5) that you enter into apps which support proxies, like browsers or downloaders. The combined “+ Psiphon” and “+ Tor” entries are hidden in Proxy mode because they route the whole device. Most users should stay in Device VPN.

The tunnel type that carries your traffic. Smart Connect automatically tests the others and picks a fast working route. WireGuard and gool are WARP-based tunnels; gool chains two WARP hops. MASQUE hides traffic inside normal-looking web traffic. WIW and MIM are two-hop variants (WARP-in-WARP and MASQUE-in-MASQUE) for stronger resistance to blocking. Entries ending “+ Psiphon” or “+ Tor” add a privacy network on top of the tunnel: your traffic first enters the tunnel, then leaves through the Psiphon or Tor network, so the sites you visit see the Psiphon/Tor exit instead of your tunnel. You do not need any separate Tor or Psiphon switch — the Protocol entry alone turns them on and off. The preset default for a new install or after Reset Defaults is WireGuard + Psiphon.

The connection method for MASQUE-based protocols, shown directly under Protocol whenever it applies. HTTP/2 (TCP) is the preset default and works on almost every network; HTTP/3 (QUIC) uses UDP and can be faster where UDP is allowed. If HTTP/3 fails to connect, Aethon automatically retries with HTTP/2. Your choice is kept even while a non-MASQUE protocol is selected.

How carefully Aethon searches for a working gateway before connecting. Turbo finds one quickly and is the best choice for daily use. Thorough, Verified and Ironclad test more gateways and check them more strictly, which can help on unreliable networks but takes longer to connect. You rarely need to change this.

How Psiphon builds its connection: Auto lets Psiphon pick the best working method; Direct avoids web-fronting methods that some networks interfere with. If Auto fails to connect, try Direct. CDN is blocked because it failed validation on this network.

The country your traffic leaves from when a “+ Psiphon” protocol is selected. Automatic picks the best available exit — the right choice for most users. Choosing a country can reduce speed if it is far away. Manual accepts any two-letter country code for countries not in the list; Psiphon decides at runtime whether it can honor it. For “+ Tor” there is no country selector: the Tor exit is chosen by the Tor network itself, and Home shows the real detected exit country read-only while connected (or “Location unavailable” while it cannot be determined — never a guess). This setting has no effect for plain protocols.

Choose which apps use the tunnel. Include: only the apps you pick go through the VPN; everything else uses the normal connection. Exclude: everything goes through the VPN except the apps you pick — useful for keeping banking apps on the local network or sending only some traffic abroad. Turn on “Show system apps” in the app picker to also list built-in Android apps; your selections are kept even when system apps are hidden. Leave Split Tunneling off to route every app through the tunnel.

Packet size for the VPN tunnel. Automatic measures what the current network can carry — leave it there unless a network drops large packets and pages stop loading; a manual value of 1280–1420 then often helps. This does not apply in Proxy mode.
All low-frequency and advanced settings, grouped by topic: Performance, Privacy & Security, Network & Routing, Proxy & Chaining, Advanced Protocols, Organization and Help.

Performance holds the recovery and timing controls. Auto Connect on Start: Aethon connects by itself when you open the app — handy if you always want protection. Quick Reconnect: after a short network loss the tunnel comes back automatically; off means you reconnect by hand. Skip Connection Check: connects without proving real traffic first — faster but you may appear connected while nothing loads; leave it off. Validation/Startup/Reconnect timeouts (seconds): how long to wait when testing a gateway, during a MASQUE handshake, and before recovery retries. Empty fields use the safe defaults; raise Startup only on very slow networks. Keep Alive: how often WireGuard sends a small packet to keep the tunnel alive; the default 5 seconds is fine, shorter uses more battery.

Obfuscation changes how WireGuard traffic looks on the network: Light, Balanced (default) and Ironclad disguise it progressively better, at some speed cost. ECH (Encrypted Client Hello) hides the website name during connection setup for MASQUE: Auto (default) uses it when supported, Off for compatibility, Custom for a trusted ECH configuration in base64. HTTP/2 Fragmentation splits the first connection message into pieces with a delay, which can defeat censorship that blocks by pattern; off by default. Kill Switch blocks all internet traffic whenever the tunnel is down, so nothing leaks — enable if you need that guarantee. Exit Location Control is unavailable in this build; leave it off.

DNS Leak Protection (on by default) sends name lookups only through the tunnel. Custom DNS: enter server IP addresses, comma-separated, to use your own name servers instead of the defaults. SNI/Host Sniffing (on by default) reads the plain connection metadata (not page contents) to match website names for the routing rules below. Block Destinations and Bypass for Destinations: one rule per line — example.com, full:example.com, keyword:ads, 10.0.0.0/8, port:25, or private. Block wins over bypass; these apply only to tunneled traffic, and app exclusions (Split Tunneling) take priority. Packet Size / MTU is explained under the Home section above.

SOCKS Address: the local SOCKS5 listener the Device VPN uses internally (default 127.0.0.1:1819); change the port only if another app occupies it. HTTP Proxy for Device VPN: an optional second local HTTP proxy (for example 127.0.0.1:1820) — must use a different port than SOCKS. Upstream Proxy: route the entire tunnel through another proxy first (socks5://, http:// or https:// URL). Connection from LAN: shares the tunnel with other devices on your Wi-Fi; enable it, then use the shown socks5:// address, port and one-time credentials in the other device’s proxy settings. In Proxy mode the fixed addresses are HTTP 127.0.0.1:1818 and SOCKS5 127.0.0.1:1819 — set either in your app.

The MASQUE connection method (HTTP/2 or HTTP/3) now lives on the main Configurations page, directly under Protocol — see the MASQUE connection method entry above. Custom Endpoint: pin a fixed gateway IP:port instead of automatic discovery — use only if you know one that works. Alternative HTTP/3 Handshake: a different QUIC opening for restricted networks; leave on unless it causes problems. Custom HTTP/2 Gateway: same idea for HTTP/2. WARP-in-WARP endpoints (outer/inner hop): override both gateways of gool’s two-hop chain — leave empty for automatic selection; hops must differ. MASQUE-in-MASQUE endpoints do the same for MIM.

For connecting with a Team (Zero Trust) account instead of a personal one. Enter the Team Name your administrator gave you, plus either an Enrollment Token or both Service Access ID and Secret. Gateway Proxy routes traffic through your organization’s gateway. Personal users leave everything empty. Credentials stay on this device and are excluded from settings backups; switching the team name switches to that team’s separate identity.

Gool Mode chooses between the two Gool designs in Aether Core v2.3.0. Gool over MASQUE (the default for new setups) carries a WireGuard WARP identity inside a MASQUE tunnel and registers it through that tunnel, so the exit address is usually foreign; the MASQUE connection method above controls its carrier (HTTP/3 or HTTP/2). Classic Gool is the older design: WireGuard inside WireGuard, a plain WARP exit; its two endpoint fields are the outer and inner hops, and naming them is what selects Classic. Upgrades from the previous version keep a saved Gool selection on Classic so the running behavior never changes silently. A working tunnel counts as connected regardless of exit country; the country shown after connecting is informational.
Encrypted Client Hello and TLS

Encrypted Client Hello (ECH) hides the server name during connection setup. Auto fetches the key automatically (Advanced: the key resolver and key domain can be changed; a resolver can be udp://, tcp://, or https://), Custom takes a trusted base64 configuration, and Off sends the name openly. If a key is required but cannot be obtained, the connection fails honestly rather than continuing without protection. TLS 1.2 Cipher Suites and TLS Key Groups shape the connection fingerprint; empty uses the built-in Chrome-like default, and an invalid value stops the connection with the option named — HTTP/3 ignores cipher suites. GREASE adds random-looking filler values for a more realistic fingerprint and is on by default. TLS Certificate Verification checks MASQUE gateways against the built-in Cloudflare certificate pins — it is pin-based checking, not standard authority validation. Split inside the server name (fragmentation only) changes where the ClientHello is split.
Identity and expert timing

WARP API Enrollment Address overrides where key registration calls go — leave empty unless you know a reachable address of the key service; with the default, a working name lookup decides. Replace Refused Identity re-registers a fresh identity automatically when Cloudflare refuses the saved one (on by default). Performance Profile (Auto, Low, Medium, High) overrides the Core’s automatic resource choice. Expert timeouts: Connection Open (default 30 seconds) bounds how long a connection through the tunnel may take to open; HTTP/2 Keepalive and its timeout (15/20) and the WireGuard endpoint cooldown (300) and tunnel silence limit (10) match the Core defaults — change them only for diagnosed problems. Core Traffic Statistics Log is diagnostic logging only; the on-screen download, upload, and time counters are measured independently and stay authoritative.
Light, Dark or System default appearance. Applies immediately.
English or Persian. The whole interface, including layout direction, switches immediately.
Notification permission and importance; the connection notification is required for the VPN to keep running in the background.
Adds an Aethon connect/disconnect tile to the quick settings panel above the notification shade.

Check for updates, download and install them. Automatic Updates checks quietly in the background and downloads on Wi-Fi. The current build may be a development build while the checked release is the latest public release.

Export writes your settings to a JSON file you choose (organization credentials and upstream proxy URLs are excluded); Import restores them on this or another device. Useful before reinstalling or moving phones.

Restores every configuration setting to Aethon’s defaults (Protocol, Scan Mode, Psiphon transport and region, and all advanced settings). Your app data, connection history and update files are untouched, and your language and theme choice are kept. A confirmation appears before anything resets.
